title: Prostrations
hook: full-length bows, done by the hundred and thousand

segments.voice: Yesterday, the guidelines, and the last of the seven points. Your line was one intention. Did you read it again last night, and how did the day look? Day one thousand three hundred four.

There's a kind of bow that leaves nothing standing. Palms come together. Then the knees go down, then the hands slide forward along the ground, and the whole body lies flat, forehead to the floor, arms stretched out ahead. A breath. Then all of it reverses: hands back, knees, feet, standing again. And then, in front of temples and in quiet shrine rooms in Tibetan Buddhist communities, people do it again, and again, and again. Some keep a pair of smooth wooden boards under their hands so they can slide. Today, the bow that uses the whole body.
screen: `A BOW THAT LEAVES NOTHING STANDING.` → `FLAT ON THE GROUND, ARMS AHEAD.` → `AND THEN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: First, how it's done. In Tibetan teachings the joined palms often touch three places before the body goes down: the crown of the head, the throat, the heart. Teachers link them to body, speech and mind. So the bow isn't only a body going down. It's the whole person, offered. Second, why the body. Pride is something you can feel in your posture: chest out, chin up, standing over things. A full prostration is the body doing the opposite, on purpose. Teachers describe it as a remedy for pride, and say the mind tends to follow where the body goes. Third, by the hundred and the thousand. In the Tibetan foundational practices, which tomorrow's lesson opens up, prostrations are done together with taking refuge, the turn met earlier with the lamrim. Practitioners picture the Buddha, the teaching and the community in front of them, and bow to them. Tradition sets a very large number, and people work through it over months or years, a session at a time. Some pilgrims even travel by prostration, measuring a road with the length of their own bodies. Fourth, all the way down. A half bow stops where it's comfortable. This one goes to the floor, where there's no further to fall. And then it gets up. Teachers point out that rising matters as much as going down: you don't stay on the ground, you return to standing, lighter, and begin again. All the way down, all the way up.
screen: `CROWN, THROAT, HEART.` · `THE BODY UNDOES PRIDE.` · `BOWED WITH REFUGE, OVER AND OVER.` · `TO THE FLOOR, AND UP AGAIN.` · then, large: `ALL THE WAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: if your body allows it, do three prostrations. Find a clear patch of floor, or a rug. Stand. Join your palms, and touch them to the crown, the throat, the heart. Then kneel, slide your hands forward, and lie flat for one breath. Come back up slowly. Three times, no rush. If a full bow isn't right for your knees or your back, kneel and bow your forehead toward the floor, or simply bow your head where you sit. Then rest in the stillness after the third one. The bell holds the time.
Prostrations. Full-length bows, the whole body to the ground, done over and over in Tibetan practice. Today's word.
Your line: all the way down. Today, when you notice yourself standing over something, a person, an argument, a job, let your shoulders drop one notch. Day one thousand three hundred four.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists do full-length prostrations in temples, shrine rooms and on pilgrimage, often reciting refuge while they bow, and as part of the foundational practices students complete them in large numbers over months or years.

original.note: Tibetan chaktsal: to prostrate, to pay homage. It's the word for this bow, and it opens many Tibetan verses of praise.

trapdoor: what you thought: bowing is a polite nod.
what it means: a full-length prostration, the whole body to the ground, offered with body, speech and mind, then rising again.
what a scholar hears: Tibetan chaktsal, homage. in the foundational practices it's joined to refuge and repeated in large numbers as a remedy for pride.

notes: Joined palms at crown, throat and heart linked to body, speech and mind: confirm as a common Tibetan instruction (practice varies).
'Tradition sets a very large number' deliberately avoids a figure; the ngondro count is commonly 100,000 (plus extras in some lineages). Keeper may decide whether to state it.
Pilgrims who travel by prostration: stated with 'some'. Confirm wording.
Prostration as a remedy for pride: confirm as a fair summary of teaching.

Original game: Tibetan ཕྱག་འཚལ (phyag 'tshal), pronounced roughly chak-tsel. The guide asks for Devanagari for Buddhism; Tibetan script is used here because the practice and word are Tibetan. Confirm spelling and choice.
